items.headline: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
items.blurb: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is "strange" Trump has described Vladimir Putin as a friend.
items.text: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks. In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend". "Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English. "He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during WWII. Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States. Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv. items.headline: Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
items.blurb: The South American country's Senate also advances proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of 2027 presidential race.
items.text: Argentina’s legislature has pushed forward a series of bills that would implement changes sought by President Javier Milei , including barring the Central Bank from printing extra money for government expenses. On Thursday, the Argentinian Chamber of Deputies gave final approval to a bill imposing restrictions on the Central Bank, defining its “primary and fundamental mission” as maintaining the value of the country’s currency. Under past administrations, the Central Bank has printed additional funds to help cover government expenses, contributing to the country’s once sky-high inflation, which reached more than 200 percent in 2023. Milei, a libertarian economist, swept into office that year on a promise to tame runaway inflation and slash government spending. Under his leadership, inflation has declined, though poverty has surged. Economists also believe Argentina may be drifting into a recession, with economic activity diminished in recent months. Still, Milei’s office celebrated the Senate’s passage of the Central Bank bill with a presidential statement. “This marks the end of nearly two decades of political manipulation at the Central Bank,” the statement said. It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association. Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights. “These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. items.text: A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US. More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. More than 400 flights in the US were cancelled on Thursday and another 2,200 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said. The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast. Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states. On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding. items.text: Georgian police have clashed with fans of Turkiye’s Besiktas after they unfurled a Palestinian flag during a Europa League game against Israel’s Hapoel Beer-Sheva. The clashes resulted in a suspension of about 30 minutes during the 26th minute of the game held in Batumi, Georgia, but it resumed after the interruption on Thursday. Besiktas eventually won 2–1. Turkish media outlets reported that Georgian police entered the stands and used pepper spray against fans of the Istanbul giant, prompting Danish referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0–0. The game was relocated by UEFA to Batumi after Turkish authorities said Istanbul could not host it for safety and security reasons. Unlike two previous Hapoel away games, spectators were allowed in the stadium. Besiktas accused Georgian police of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game. “We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the Turkish club said in a statement. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.” The

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the public prosecutor’s office said in a statement. The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the health ministry. At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb. The Egyptian president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sissi , expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. items.headline: Israeli settlers damage Palestinian family’s homes in West Bank attack
items.blurb: The Tubasi family was forced out months ago and has been denied a return by settlers despite an Israeli court order.
items.text: Israeli settlers have smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the occupied West Bank after attacks stopped the family from returning. Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the two-storey houses in the village of Jaloud, near Nablus, at about 1am on Thursday (23:00 GMT on Wednesday), before starting to damage them, Reuters reported. It added that the concrete foundations of the homes had been partially broken. “This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators,” said Ghiath Nasser, the owners’ lawyer. The Israeli military said the attack was “a serious criminal act” and said it was investigating, despite settlers remaining in the vicinity throughout the day. The Tubasi family now live in a small house in Jaloud with a direct view of the homes they fled. “They want to demolish the houses so that we cannot return to them,” Wael Tubasi, one of the owners, said. He said the deadline for the military to remove the settlers had passed.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports. The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees. items.headline: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
items.blurb: Nearly a third of crossings in early 2026 allegedly involved boats or engines from the German man's firm.
items.text: A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal. Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen. The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges. His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died. We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police. Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty. The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case.

items.text: Kannur ( Keralam ), Nov 26: A case was on Thursday registered against CPI(M) district secretariat member T I Madhusoodanan on a complaint alleging that he made a provocative speech at a public meeting organised by the DYFI in Payyannur recently. The FIR has been registered under sections 192 (wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot), 351 (criminal intimidation) and 352 (intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita on a complaint by Kerala Students Union state vice president P Muhammed Shammas to the state police chief. According to the complaint, Madhusoodanan at the DYFI event held in Payyannur as part of the Koothuparamba Martyrs' Day celebrations, allegedly made a speech which could disrupt the peace and incite the opposing party's members to a riot. Earlier in the day, state Home Minister Ramesh Chenithala had said the Home Department was taking the remarks seriously and that the police were collecting the full text of the speech for examination. items.text: Uttar Pradesh government on Thursday (November 26, 2026) appointed senior Indian Police Service (IPS) officer Alok Singh, as chairman of the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission (UPPSC). Mr. Singh, a 1995-batch IPS officer from U.P. cadre is currently serving as Director General (DG), Pradeshik Armed Constabulary (PAC). His tenure as Chairman UPPSC will continue until Jan 23, 2029, as per the govt notification. “Using the power confer under Article 316 (Part 1) of the Constitution of India, the Governor appoints Shri Alok Singh, DG, PAC, as Chairman Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission (UPPSC). His tenure will continue until Jan 23, 2029,” reads the official notification. Sanjay Shrinet, the outgoing Chairman of Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission (UPPSC) completed his tenure of more than five years as Chairman of the commission on November 21. items.text: The promoters of Kerala-based Kalyan Silks are exploring a minority stake sale that could value the textile retailer at ₹ 2,500–3,000 crore even as it considers a public listing, two people familiar with the matter said. The deal may involve a 20% stake sale, with the capital likely to be a mix of primary and secondary share sales, the first of the two persons cited earlier said, both speaking on the condition of anonymity. Kalyan Silks has hired Mumbai-based investment bank O3 Capital to arrange the transaction, the second person said. A profitable company, Kalyan Silks is currently focused on strengthening its financials after repeated attempts to secure a deal with multiple investors failed. Emails sent to Kalyan Silks and O3 Capital did not elicit a response until press time. A successful deal will mark the first round of external fundraising by the company, which is also exploring options for a public listing. items.headline: Australian shares set for best week since August as financials, WiseTech rally
items.blurb: AUSTRALIA-STOCKS/ MIDDAY:Australian shares set for best week since August as financials, WiseTech rally
items.text: Nov 27 (Reuters) - Australian shares edged higher on Friday and were on track for their best week since early August, buoyed by financials and WiseTech Global after the software firm reaffirmed its annual revenue targets. The S&P/ASX 200 index was up 0.4% at 8,796.2 points, as of 2320 GMT. The benchmark has gained 2.4% so far this week, slowly recovering from a 5% decline last week, its worst showing since June 2022. Sector heavyweight WiseTech Global drove technology stocks 3% higher, with its shares soaring 20% after the CFO voiced confidence in meeting its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast, putting the stock on course for its strongest session in more than two years. Financials gained 0.5% and were set for a 1.1% weekly rise. National Australia Bank and ANZ Group were the only "Big Four" banks in positive territory. Energy stocks gained roughly 1% as crude prices settled firmer after mine strikes and an attack on a refinery reignited concerns about global supply disruptions. Shares of Woodside Energy climbed as much as 2.1% to their strongest level since early November.

items.headline: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat

items.text: There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week. Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations. "We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC. Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda. The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April. items.blurb: Global investment firm Norwest Venture Partners has offloaded a 2.15% stake in SaaS company Amagi through a block deal worth Rs 262.44 crore. According to exchange data, Norwest Venture Partners X Mauritius sold 47.37 lakh shares at Rs 554 each on the NSE.
items.text: Global investment firm Norwest Venture Partners has offloaded a 2.15% stake in SaaS company Amagi through a block deal worth Rs 262.44 crore. According to exchange data, Norwest Venture Partners X Mauritius sold 47.37 lakh shares at Rs 554 each on the NSE. The transaction was executed at a discount of around 3% to Amagi's previous closing price of Rs 571.05 per share. On the buying side, Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund acquired 33.27 lakh shares worth Rs 184.33 crore. Old Bridge Capital Management's All Cap Strategy picked up 7.65 lakh shares worth Rs 42.38 crore, while Long Term Equity Fund acquired 6.45 lakh shares worth Rs 35.73 crore. items.headline: AI is straining America’s open records systems
items.blurb: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer.
items.text: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy. Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.” Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest.

items.headline: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
items.blurb: Frontier AI is already solving problems that once took top physicists a full day.
items.text: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics. LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online. The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset. It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math. The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. items.headline: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
items.blurb: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
items.text: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. items.headline: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
items.blurb: Most codes of conduct serve as a reflection of corporate culture. In Nvidia's case, that could have consequences.
items.text: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO. It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for.
